note: Account audit prepared for Jason Brown by Zee.Media, September 2026. Figures are from your own Klaviyo and Recharge data.

data.name: Human Improvement

audit.sub: Where the account is leaking and where the upside is. Built from your own Klaviyo and Recharge data over the twelve complete months to August 2026. Figures are Klaviyo-attributed unless noted, and the store total is every Shopify order Klaviyo tracks. Prepared for Jason Brown by Zee.Media.

wins.title: Build the subscription retention layer
wins.detail: Recharge fires 2,747 failed charges, 6,601 upcoming-charge notices and 2,577 cancellations a year, and not one of the eight subscription flows exists to answer them. Dunning on the failed charges, a skip-or-delay offer before the charge, and a win-back after cancellation are the three highest-value emails missing from the account.

wins.title: Make second orders happen
wins.detail: 16,272 people have bought, 4,840 have bought twice, so roughly 70% never came back. There is no bounce-back flow after a first order and no email win-back at all; the only win-back running is two SMS that earned $241 in twelve months.

wins.title: Push more first orders onto subscription
wins.detail: 4,088 subscriptions started in the last year and 7,268 of your orders are subscription orders. The post-purchase flow that pushes a first-time buyer onto subscription went live in August and is the right idea; it needs the rest of the lifecycle behind it.

wins.title: Turn one campaign a week into three
wins.detail: 84 real campaigns went out in twelve months, about 1.7 a week once the 28 resends are set aside, and each one earns about $220. The list is growing by 18,506 a year and is being asked to buy far less often than it could be.

wins.title: Re-open the abandonment flows sooner
wins.detail: Site abandonment will not re-open for 45 days and browse for 30. A repeat abandoner inside that window is invisible to the flow. Four to seven days is the standard we use, and it is a settings change rather than a build.

wins.title: Test the popup, and the offer behind it
wins.detail: Two forms are live out of twenty, and not one of them has ever run an A/B test. Capture is already the strongest part of the account at 18,506 new subscribers a year, which is exactly why it is worth testing rather than leaving alone.

audit.title: Account audit

findings.body:
You said three things: email is under-indexing below 10% of revenue, subscription churn is higher than you want, and one-time buyers are not coming back. All three are true, all three are measurable in your account, and all three have the same cause.

1. Email is 9.9% of revenue. $57,892 of a $584,598 store over the last twelve months. You were right to the decimal. Two accounts we manage sit at 33.7% and 36.8%. The gap between 10% and a conservative 25% is about $88,258 a year.

2. Subscription churn. 4,088 subscriptions started in the last twelve months and 2,577 cancelled, so for every 100 you win you lose about 63. Worse, 2,747 charges failed in the same period, which is more than the number of people who chose to leave. There is no email anywhere in the account that responds to a failed charge, an upcoming charge, a pause or a cancellation.

3. One-time buyers. 16,272 people have ordered, 4,840 have ordered twice. That is a 30% repeat rate, so about 70% never came back. There is no bounce-back flow after a first order, no replenishment reminder, and no email win-back.

The common cause. Your acquisition flows are built and running: welcome, browse, cart, checkout, site, post-purchase, all six of them live. Everything that holds on to a customer after the second week is either a draft or absent. That is why all three symptoms show up at once, and it is also why they can be fixed together.

chart.leak: Each stage is where the account stands today against what we would expect from a subscription business this size.

findings.title: Your three questions, answered

findings.body:
The store did $584,598 over the last twelve months and roughly doubled on the year, from about $25,000 a month in mid-2025 to $55,000 to $65,000 now. Email and SMS drove $57,892 of it, or 9.9%.

A well-run lifecycle and campaign programme usually drives 25% to 35% of store revenue. Two accounts we manage sit at 33.7% and 36.8%, and both sell a consumable the way you do. Lifting you from 9.9% to 25%, which is the bottom of the healthy band rather than the top, is worth about $88,258 a year at today's store size, and more as the store grows.

The wins below add up to about $108,106 a year. We have kept every estimate deliberately low and priced each one off your own numbers rather than a benchmark.
findings.title: Email is 9.9% of a $584,598 store

findings.body:
18,506 people joined the email list in the last twelve months against 4,596 unsubscribes, so you netted 13,910. Your unsubscribe rate is 0.34% and spam complaints run around 0.02%, which is well inside safe. Deliverability is not your problem and the list is not tired.

That matters because it means the gap is not acquisition. You are filling the top of the funnel faster than most accounts this size and then asking those people to buy about once a week, with nothing to catch them after they order.
findings.title: Capture is genuinely strong, and that is the foundation

findings.body:
The account holds 20 forms. Two are live, the desktop and mobile halves of one popup. The other eighteen are drafts, including a 15% multi-step and a free-creatine offer that were built and never shipped.

Not one form in the account has an A/B test on it. For a business adding 18,506 subscribers a year, the popup is the highest-traffic asset you own and it has never been challenged. Offer, timing, and the multi-step versus single-step question are all cheap tests with compounding value, because every extra subscriber flows through the welcome series and everything after it.
findings.title: Two forms live out of twenty, and no form has ever been tested

findings.body:
Recharge is fully integrated and firing every event you would want. In the last twelve months it recorded 4,088 subscriptions started, 2,577 cancelled, 167 paused, 2,747 charges failed and 6,601 upcoming-charge notices. Nothing in Klaviyo is listening to any of it.

Failed charges are the biggest single leak. 2,747 in a year is more than the 2,577 people who actively chose to leave. Recharge retries a card on its own schedule, but nobody emails the customer to fix it, so a subscription ends because of an expired card rather than a decision. Every serious subscription brand runs a dunning sequence here, and it is usually the fastest money in the account.

Then the charge nobody warns about. 6,601 upcoming-charge events fired and none of them sent an email. That email is not a courtesy, it is where a customer presses skip or pushes the date out instead of cancelling, which is exactly the leak below.

And nobody asks them back. 35 subscriptions reactivated against 2,577 cancellations, which is 1.4%. A cancelled subscriber is the warmest audience you will ever email and the account has never emailed them.

chart.note: Everything on this chart already happens in Recharge. None of it triggers an email.
Measured against the subscription layer we build for every subscription client.

findings.title: None of the eight subscription flows exist, and Recharge is already talking

findings.body:
Your cancellation segments carry the reason people gave. After the 1,767 who gave no reason, the largest group is surplus: 792 people cancelled because they had too much product. Price was 262, no results 97, and taste 85.

Surplus is the cheapest churn there is to fix, because the customer still wants the product. They just want it later. Recharge already supports skip, delay and frequency change, and 355 people found those settings by themselves last year. An email before each charge offering to push it back converts a cancellation into a pause, and the subscription survives.

It also explains the pause numbers: 167 paused against 2,577 cancelled. When the only visible button is cancel, people cancel.
findings.title: The top cancellation reason is having too much product

findings.body:
2,006 people are on an active Recharge subscription today. The cancelled segments hold 3,003, so there are more former subscribers than current ones. That is normal for a business that has been selling subscriptions for years without a retention programme, and it is also a standing asset: a list of people who have already trusted you with a recurring charge.

Subscription orders were 7,268 of the 10,296 orders you took in the last twelve months, so 71% of your order volume. The health of that base is the health of the business, which is why we would start here rather than with campaigns.

chart.note: Counts, not rates. The cancelled pool is larger than the active one, and only a handful have ever come back.

findings.title: 2,006 active subscribers, and a bigger pile of cancelled ones

findings.body:
16,272 people have placed an order. 4,840 have placed two or more. That is a 30% repeat rate, and it is the number behind what you described as a big fall-off of one-time orderers.

Nothing in the account is built to change it. There is no bounce-back flow, which is the email that goes out a couple of weeks after a first order with a reason to come back. There is no replenishment reminder timed to when a tub actually runs out, which for a powder is the single most natural email a brand can send. And the only win-back running is two SMS messages that earned $241 in twelve months.

You also have 6,047 people sitting in a 120-day lapsed win-back segment that somebody built and never connected to anything, and 54,949 people who have never bought at all. That is a large, already-owned audience with no programme pointed at it.
findings.title: 70% of your buyers have bought exactly once

findings.body:
There are 102 flows in the account. 12 are live. The rest are drafts going back to 2021, left behind by at least two previous teams: the SS | set was built between June and August this year, the KLN - set in 2025, and underneath both there are a dozen abandoned-cart variants and twenty-odd welcome flows.

Measured against the framework we build to, the split is stark. Core acquisition is 6 of 6 live and in reasonable shape. The advanced retention layer is 1 of 12. The subscription layer is 0 of 8.

The drafts are also a live risk rather than just clutter. Several duplicate cart and welcome flows are one toggle away from double-sending to the same person, and a name like (DONT USE) KLN - Abandoned Cart Reminder is only a warning while whoever wrote it still works there.

live: Post Purchase (first time buyer to subscription push)
chart.note: Against the flow framework we build for every client. Subscription flows are counted separately in the section above.

findings.title: 12 flows live, 88 drafts, and the retention half is missing

findings.body:
Credit where it is due: the welcome, cart, checkout, browse and site flows were all rebuilt between June and August 2026, and the early numbers are good. The new welcome series earns $0.57 a recipient against $0.26 for the one it replaced, which is more than double.

Across all flows you earn $0.55 a recipient. Two accounts we manage sit at $0.74 and $0.77, so you are behind but in the same league, and those accounts have the full retention layer feeding the average. Your flows are not underperforming so much as under-deployed: $29,752 a year out of 12 flows, where the same framework built out fully would be running twenty-plus.

chart.note: Flow revenue per recipient, against two accounts we manage. Same category, consumable products, both with the full retention layer built.

findings.title: The rebuilt core flows are working, and they are only weeks old

findings.body:
Re-entry decides whether the same person can come back through a flow. Yours are set long: site abandonment will not re-open for 45 days, browse for 30, and cart and checkout for 14. We build these at four to seven days.

The effect is invisible in the reporting because the entries simply never happen. Someone who browses twice in a fortnight gets one browse email, and a subscription customer who abandons a cart every month gets a cart flow once a quarter. For a consumable with a monthly rhythm, a 30 to 45 day lock is close to switching the flow off between orders.

This is a settings change, not a build, which makes it the cheapest item on the list.
findings.title: Every abandonment flow waits too long before it re-opens

findings.body:
Sorted by revenue over the last twelve months. Worth noticing that the two biggest earners are welcome flows, which is what an account looks like when the only working programme is the one that greets people. The post-purchase education flows reach a lot of people for very little: the MSM flow delivered 12,165 emails for $248.

Nothing here is broken. It is thin, and the thin part is everything that happens after someone becomes a customer.
findings.title: Every flow at a glance

findings.body:
84 real campaigns went out over the last twelve months, plus 28 resends to non-openers, so roughly 1.7 genuine sends a week. They earned $28,140 from 1,350,260 recipients, which is $0.0189 a recipient and a 0.032% placed-order rate.

Two accounts we manage earn $0.057 and $0.082 a recipient on campaigns, so the gap is three to four times rather than a few percent. The cause is not the list: your unsubscribe and complaint rates are healthy, so people are not angry, they are just not being given enough reasons to buy.

Six of your sends in the window earned exactly nothing on 11,000 to 12,000 recipients each, including two sends aimed at a non-engaged segment. Those are worth retiring rather than repeating.

chart.note: Campaign revenue per recipient, against two accounts we manage.

findings.title: About 1.7 campaigns a week, at $0.0189 a recipient

findings.body:
28 of the 112 sends were resends to people who did not open the first email. They earned $0.0319 a recipient against $0.0189 for a full campaign, so about 68% more.

That is unusual and it tells you something useful: the content is fine and the problem is reach and frequency. When you put the same email in front of people a second time it works harder than the first attempt did. Keep them, and read it as permission to send more often rather than less.
findings.title: Your resends earn more per person than your campaigns do

findings.body:
Engagement tiers, as your own segments define them: 19,321 people have clicked, ordered or subscribed in the last 120 days, and 14,790 have done nothing for a year. A typical campaign reaches about 12,056 people.

So the campaign audience is a reasonable slice of the engaged core, which is correct practice and protects deliverability. The opportunity is the other direction: there are 54,949 profiles who have never bought, and the only thing currently speaking to them is the welcome series and a weekly campaign.

chart.note: Your own engagement segments, plus the average campaign reach.
chart.freqHead: How often each tier hears from you

findings.title: Where the list sits, and who is being left out

findings.body:
We checked properly rather than assuming. None of the 20 forms has an A/B test on it, and we could not find a single live or completed experiment on the live flows. The SMS side is the same picture: $4,131 of SMS revenue from 7,827 messages in twelve months, with no testing behind it.

That is not a criticism of whoever built the flows, it is simply the stage the account is at. But it does mean every number in this audit is a first draft: nobody has yet tried a second version of the popup, the welcome offer, a subject line or a send time. Our own win rate across accounts sits around two thirds, and the compounding from testing is usually larger than any single flow we build.

chart.themSub: tests found across 12 live flows and 20 forms

findings.title: Nothing in the account is being tested

findings.body:
Here is the short version of this audit. You have a healthy store growing fast, strong list growth, clean deliverability, and a competent set of acquisition flows that were rebuilt this winter. What you do not have is a retention programme, and you are a subscription business, which is why all three of the problems in your email show up at the same time.

The work is not glamorous. It is a dunning sequence, a pre-charge email with a skip button, a cancellation save, a win-back, a bounce-back, a replenishment reminder, a re-entry setting changed from 45 days to 7, and then a testing rhythm on top so the whole thing keeps improving instead of sitting still. Built once, it runs whether anyone is watching or not, and it compounds into a retention system that does not falter.

We work with brands doing roughly $3M to $20M, and the pattern above is the one we see most often: acquisition solved, retention untouched. On your own numbers the items in this audit come to about $108,106 a year, which would put email at roughly 28% of revenue and inside the normal band for the first time.
